title: How Veteran Teachers Keep Their Cool
author: Paige Tutt
summary: Paige Tutt gathers advice from about a dozen experienced educators on staying emotionally regulated when everyday student misbehavior pushes a teacher's buttons. The central claim, voiced by educational neuroscientist Lori Desautels, is that teachers must first notice their own heightened emotions and recalibrate so their response stays proportional to the behavior, acting like a thermostat that holds a steady temperature. Michael Linsin adds an important caveat: composure only works alongside solid classroom management. The strategies are concrete: a three-second pause to choose a response, imagining an audience or a child's parents watching, a desk reminder reading "Discipline without emotion," co-regulating with a student or taking a class walk, choosing a later private moment to address a hurtful comment, and Jennifer Gonzalez's practice of stopping to write frustrations and then what is going well. The article closes with repair, including apologising to students when a teacher oversteps and reflecting afterward on personal triggers, and with a veteran's view that projecting high expectations through tone and body language steadies both teacher and class.
points: Self-regulation begins with awareness of one's own sensations, allowing a response proportional to the misbehavior rather than a reflexive one.
Composure is presented as complementary to, not a replacement for, effective classroom management systems.
Simple cognitive reframes, such as imagining the child's parents watching, help teachers show up as their best selves under pressure.
Addressing a hurtful student comment later and privately, while naming its impact, can model empathy more effectively than an immediate retort.
Apologising when a teacher oversteps and reflecting on personal triggers afterward are framed as essential repair and preparation for future incidents.
quotes: The trick to short-circuiting—or at least reducing the likelihood of—a reflexive, potentially regrettable response, veteran teachers told us, is to develop the ability to recognize heightened emotions as soon as they surface and then quickly recalibrate (pause, breathe, take a sip of water, step away) so the teacher response is proportional to the student misbehavior.
Of course, as beneficial as teacher composure is, veteran teacher Linsin notes, it’s only one part of keeping a classroom afloat when student behavior is pushing your buttons.

This doesn’t require a deep meditation, “just three seconds,” adds educational consultant Chandna Mukherjee. To prevent a knee-jerk reaction to challenging behaviors, Mukherjee recommends that teachers ask themselves, How do I want to respond? That pause ensures that your next steps are deliberate.

Instead of reacting harshly in the moment, Plotinsky emphasizes the impact of choosing the right time to respond to certain student behaviors—whether that’s one-on-one at the end of class, or even a few days later.
Quickly venting, then shifting her perspective and taking stock of what was working, allowed Gonzalez to realign her focus before helping the classroom get back on track.
Occasionally stepping up to say, “I’m sorry, let’s fix this,” provides an important lesson in acknowledging mistakes and taking accountability, says fifth-grade teacher Nita Creekmore
We might sit down and write out a referral or write out some documentation, but we don’t always look at ‘what stuff was coming up for me?
